verdicts.trueWording: "it is geometric rather than power law" (Abstract)
verdicts.note: Live PNAS blocked by Cloudflare (403); read via Wayback raw capture 20250710185328id_. Abstract: 'the distribution of intervals between significant deaths in chapters is different to that for the in-story timeline; it is geometric rather than power law.' Authorship confirmed on page: Thomas Gessey-Jones, Connaughton, Dunbar, Kenna, MacCarron, O'Conchobhair, Yose, PNAS 117(46) 28582-28588, 2 Nov 2020. Results section independently confirms the geometric fit is 'the superior description of interevent times in discourse'.

verdicts.trueWording: "if they directly meet each other or it is explicitly clear from the text they knew one another"
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Sentence sits in the Materials and Methods body (heading at line 126, text at 127): 'characters are deemed to have interacted if they directly meet each other or it is explicitly clear from the text they knew one another, even if one or both are dead by that point in the story.' Quote fragment verbatim; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "Martin uses an argument from 'authenticity' to justify his relegation of women..."
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Opening body paragraph: 'the main thrust of Carroll's argument is that Martin uses an argument from "authenticity" to justify his relegation of women to traditional female roles, the validation of men through violence, and the depiction of non-Westerosi characters through tropes long associated in Western literature with "Orientalism".' Quote verbatim; the claim's compression to 'treatment of women, violence and non-Westerosi characters' fairly renders the three named targets. Byline Don Riggs, Fafnir 6.2, pp. 73-75, confirmed on page.

verdicts.trueWording: "his overarching way of reimaginging the Middle Ages-is violent, dark, brutal, and relentlessly masculine"
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Opening sentence of the section headed 'Fantasy for People Who Hate Fantasy', exactly as the claim's page field states. Quote 'violent, dark, brutal, and relentlessly masculine' verbatim. Byline on page: Shiloh Carroll, 15 May 2018 (claim says 2018).

verdicts.trueWording: "something fundamentally dishonest if you write a war story and you leave that out"
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). In the section headed 'A Savage Beast in Every Man', Carroll introduces the block quote with 'Even Martin argues that rape is necessary to his story he's telling, especially in times of war:' then quotes Martin: 'When I read history books, rape is a part of all these wars... It just seems to me that there's something fundamentally dishonest if you write a war story and you leave that out.' Quote verbatim; the antecedent of 'that' is rape, so the claim's 'leave rape out' is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "forcing the author to describe and explain what is seen by the point of view character"
verdicts.note: PDF fetched (200) and text extracted with pypdf (9 pages). Introduction, 'The Portal-Quest Fantasy' section: 'In the quest fantasy we see the world through this transitional narrative: for despite the assertion that this world has always existed, the technique remains identical to that of the portal fantasy and the effect on the language of the text is the same, forcing the author to describe and explain what is seen by the point of view character as s/he negotiates the world.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 'Chapter 3: "Look with Your Eyes" - Immersion and Thinning'
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Routledge listing for 'George R.R. Martin and the Fantasy Form' by Joseph Young (Routledge, copyright 2019, 230pp) lists in its Table of Contents: 'Chapter 3: "Look with Your Eyes" - Immersion and Thinning' (page uses an en dash where the claim uses a hyphen). Quote verbatim; chapter number, title and authorship all supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "the first four books of ASOIAF are rendered searchable in their entirety"
verdicts.note: Live WordPress host served a JS bot challenge (403); read via Wayback raw capture 20170726070428id_. Abstract, second paragraph: 'In order to explore these questions, this talk introduces the concept of corpus linguistic analysis. With the aid of contemporary software, the first four books of ASOIAF are rendered searchable in their entirety, and quantifiable patterns of language can be extracted.' Quote verbatim; byline 'Matthew Voice, University of Sheffield' and the 2014 Nine Worlds abstract posting (15 Aug 2014) confirmed on the capture.

verdicts.trueWording: "they pored over 10,000 pages of novels, pulling out all references to history, myths and legends"
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Feature body: 'Elio M. Garcia and Linda Antonsson, founders of the fan site Westeros.org... As co-writers, they pored over 10,000 pages of novels, pulling out all references to history, myths and legends. After they organized and formed the book's structure, Martin stepped in to fill in the blanks.' Quote verbatim; 'Interview by Cat Acree' and 'originally published in the December 2014 issue of BookPage' both on page.

verdicts.trueWording: "I was supposed to write 50,000 words of text for sidebars, and then I wrote 300,000!"
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Article body: '"I was supposed to write 50,000 words of text for sidebars, and then I wrote 300,000!" Martin told us recently, laughing over a slice of pizza.' Quote verbatim; page carries the byline Jennifer Vineyard and the line 'This article originally appeared in Vulture,' supporting the 'told Vulture' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: "setting your narrative atop this iceberg of history, using that background to give your text solidity"
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Essay body: 'It's an interesting idea, setting your narrative atop this iceberg of history, using that background to give your text solidity.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported. Authorship: the essay pages carry no byline, but their parent index (atseajournal.com/asoiaf/, fetched raw) is headed 'A Study of Ice and Fire / Erik Germani'.

verdicts.trueWording: "It's a big part of why the world feels so lived-in... Everyone had a life before page one."
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Essay body: 'It's a big part of why the world feels so lived-in, this rich and continuous history. Everyone had a life before page one.' Quote verbatim; the lived-in limb and the before-page-one limb are adjacent sentences. Same Germani attribution route as index 808.

verdicts.trueWording: "Martin keeps us turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences"
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Essay body: 'To that end, Martin keeps us turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences. It's shotgun writing...' Quote verbatim (claim renders the page's 'us' as 'readers' in its own prose, not inside the quotation). Attribution via the parent index byline 'Erik Germani'.

verdicts.trueWording: "Most fantasists settle for a few linguistic relics to give a historical veneer"
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Essay body: 'Most fantasists settle for a few linguistic relics to give a historical veneer... Martin has a few of these, like the much-teased "must needs". There's also "soon or late", "pretend to surprise", and "near as" for "nearly as".' Quote verbatim; all three archaisms the claim names are on the page (the page names a fourth, 'pretend to surprise', which the claim's 'among Martin's' does not exclude).

verdicts.trueWording: "What we need to do is build cultures, not worlds. And before anything else, culture is a language, a voice."
verdicts.note: Fetched live (200). Essay body, consecutive sentences: 'What we need to do is build cultures, not worlds. And before anything else, culture is a language, a voice.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported. The 'we' is writers/worldbuilders in context ('Worldbuilding aficionados overemphasize week one of the Almighty's to-do list').
